description: Self-healing data pipeline that uses an LLM to classify schema drift, reroute broken streams, and auto-generate recovery migrations without human intervention
opening_quip: Superintendent Chalmers asked me to be fair, and fair I shall be — Team Conduit has produced a pipeline that heals itself, which is more than I can say for the boiler in C-wing, which has been broken since February and which Groundskeeper Willie assures me is 'more of a philosophical problem.'

dimensions.name: Architecture
dimensions.subtitle: Code structure, layering, and separation of concerns
dimensions.evidence: pipeline/, classifier/, migrator/, and api/ packages with clear boundaries. Source, transform, and sink are interface types in pipeline/contract.go. The LLM classifier is injected as a dependency; tests swap in a stub. Some controller logic bleeds into the HTTP handlers but overall separation is sound.
dimensions.quip: The dependency injection is textbook and the interface design is sensible — I dock one point for the handler leak, which I note not to penalise but because a rubric without consequence is merely a suggestion.

dimensions.name: Integrations
dimensions.subtitle: External systems wired together and called at runtime
dimensions.evidence: Kafka consumer + producer, PostgreSQL (pipeline state and schema registry), S3 for migration artifact storage, Claude API for schema classification, and a Slack webhook for recovery notifications. Auth via IAM role assumed at startup; no hardcoded credentials found.
dimensions.quip: Five real integrations with IAM-sourced credentials and no plaintext secrets is the kind of hygiene I ask for every year and receive perhaps once, and never twice from the same team.

dimensions.name: Problem Difficulty
dimensions.subtitle: Inherent hardness of the core problem attempted
dimensions.evidence: Schema drift detection via structural diff plus an LLM classification pass; migration generation using a template engine seeded by the LLM output. The recovery routing is rule-based with an LLM override for ambiguous cases. Core problem is well-understood but the LLM-in-the-loop recovery loop is non-trivial to make reliable.
dimensions.quip: Using an LLM to generate database migrations on a live stream is the kind of idea that sounds reckless until you read the tests, at which point it merely sounds adventurous.

dimensions.name: Scope Delivered
dimensions.subtitle: How much works end-to-end in the hackathon window
dimensions.evidence: End-to-end demo: ingest a Kafka topic with a deliberately broken schema, classify the drift, generate and apply a migration, and resume the stream — all without manual intervention. Slack alert fires on recovery. Three test pipelines running at demo time.
dimensions.quip: A self-healing pipeline that recovers live in the demo is worth more than three decks of architecture diagrams, and I say this as a man who has reviewed many architecture diagrams and very few working demos.

dimensions.name: Engineering Rigor
dimensions.subtitle: Test coverage, CI pipeline, error handling, code quality
dimensions.evidence: 52 test files; integration tests spin up Kafka + Postgres via testcontainers. CI runs golangci-lint and tests. No benchmark suite; race detector not enabled in CI. Error handling is consistent in the pipeline core but thinner in the migrator.
dimensions.quip: testcontainers against a real Kafka is commendable; the missing race detector is the sort of gap that does not matter until it suddenly matters enormously, a lesson I learned the hard way during the 2019 attendance-tracking incident.

dimensions.name: Innovation
dimensions.subtitle: Novelty and creativity of the approach or solution
dimensions.evidence: The LLM is used not for generation alone but as a classification oracle whose confidence score gates whether the template engine attempts a migration or escalates to human review. The classifier prompt is versioned alongside the code and tested with snapshot assertions.
dimensions.quip: Versioned, snapshot-tested LLM prompts treated as first-class code artifacts is a design decision I did not expect to see in a hackathon and which I will be plagiarising for my own projects immediately.

dimensions.name: Operational Readiness
dimensions.subtitle: Containerization, deployment, observability, and reproducibility
dimensions.evidence: Dockerfile present and functional. docker-compose.yml with Kafka, Zookeeper, Postgres, and the service. README covers local setup clearly. No Kubernetes manifests; no structured logging beyond stdlib log. make demo works reliably.
dimensions.quip: A working Compose stack and a reliable make demo are the bare minimum I ask for and am delighted to receive; the absence of structured logging is a gap I note with the weary resignation of a man who has given this note many times.

closing_quip: Fifty-four out of seventy. Grade: B. A solid, working submission with genuine novelty in the LLM-as-classifier design. The engineering is sound, the demo persuasive, and the recovery loop is more reliable than I initially feared. I am recommending it for commendation with the observation that a race detector and structured logging would have made it a very different conversation.
